packs.title: Canyons and Coast
packs.promise: Make three outings from a canyon classroom to hilltop parks and the southern shore.

q.s: Follow one rescue idea through the visitor yard.
st: Use the open visitor yard and its current displays; a patient sighting is a bonus.
Find one display about rescue or rehabilitation and one about ocean health.
Record one fact from each, then write a question the two facts make you want to ask. Use a display or ask an available docent without interrupting care.

q.s: Draw a view without chasing a summit.
st: Choose a comfortable public position inside the park.
Use five lines to sketch a near shape, a middle-distance shape and the farthest visible edge. A hazy day still counts.
Add three words for the weather or light, then compare your tiny drawing with the actual view.

q.s: Compose a scene with words before taking a picture.
st: Choose an open public blufftop viewpoint, leaving the path clear.
Imagine a postcard frame containing one near detail, one coastline shape and a patch of sky.
Write a two-sentence postcard describing only what is visible today, or make a quick sketch.

packs.title: Village in Detail
packs.promise: Collect art, stories and small discoveries on two connected walking afternoons.

q.s: Build a palette from the actual afternoon.
st: Choose one comfortable public viewing position.
Pick three colors from the scene and give each your own short name.
Arrange the colors as three swatches or three written lines, then add a detail that made one color stand out.

q.s: Look twice at a changing exhibition.
st: Enter the open public gallery and choose one work on view.
Describe a small detail, then step back to an ordinary viewing distance and notice how it fits the whole.
Record the displayed work reference and a sentence about what changed in your reading. Do not touch or copy the artwork.

q.s: Give a reading discovery a tiny new frame.
st: In the open library, find an available book or displayed item connected with this community.
Record its title and author or collection reference, then read a short available section.
Write your own one-sentence question inspired by it and a three-word title for your question. Do not copy a passage.
